There's no St Kilda-specific figure available, and I'd be cautious about any number presented as one. The honest answer is that "EV ready" on its own is hard to isolate as a price driver, because it usually gets bundled with broader energy features in the data.

What the available research shows:

The most-cited figures lump EV readiness in with other green features (solar, double glazing, efficient heating). On that combined basis, Melbourne units show roughly a 22% valuation premium for energy features, higher than Sydney's. But that's the whole basket, not EV charging alone, so treating 22% as the EV-ready uplift would overstate it considerably. 
Futurecharging

For EV readiness specifically, the evidence is softer and more directional. EV sales in Australia have tripled since 2021, and buyers are increasingly seeking EV-ready properties, in some cases paying a premium. The Victorian Government notes that making a building EV-ready can increase property value, and that buildings without charging risk a competitive disadvantage in resale and rental markets. That's a real but not precisely quantified effect. 
EVSE Australia
All Electric Homes

A few things that matter specifically for St Kilda:

The bigger value question for an apartment is usually whether the building is EV-ready (common-property infrastructure, strata-approved) versus just a single bay. In Victoria, installing shared EV infrastructure requires a 75% special resolution of owners, which is a genuine hurdle — so a building that has already cleared it removes a cost and headache a buyer would otherwise inherit. Retrofitting later isn't trivial: backbone infrastructure can run from around $75,000 to $200,000, plus roughly $2,000–$3,000 per connection. 
SolarQuotes
SolarQuotes

So the practical framing: in a dense, EV-adopting inner-Melbourne suburb like St Kilda, "EV ready" reads more as a downside-protection and saleability factor than a clean headline percentage. It widens your buyer pool and avoids a future retrofit cost rather than reliably adding a fixed X% to the price.

If you're weighing a specific listing, the sharper question is whether the EV readiness is building-wide and strata-approved, or just a charger you'd have to fight the owners corporation to install. First, a sanity check on the quote itself. The infrastructure cost the industry quotes for retrofitting an existing building runs roughly $75k to $200k, with individual charger connections on top at around $2-3k each. So $125k for the building-wide backbone sits squarely in the normal range, arguably the sensible middle of it. This isn't an inflated quote. And $2.5-3k for the largest lots, as a one-off capital cost, is about 0.3 to 0.5% of a typical St Kilda apartment value. Calling that "prohibitive" is a strong word for a sub-1% one-time spend on an asset worth several hundred thousand.

The reframe that usually wins these arguments is separating two things the skeptics tend to blur:

The $125k buys shared EV-ready infrastructure (cabling, switchboard capacity, conduit, load management). It does not buy everyone a charger. Individual owners only pay for their own charger, if and when they want one. So the "I'll never own an EV, why should I pay" objection is answered: the shared spend protects the building's value and saleability for everyone, while the actual EV cost stays user-pays.

The cost-of-delay point is the other strong card. If the building doesn't do this collectively, you don't avoid the problem, you just hit it messily later. The classic failure mode is residents installing chargers ad hoc until the switchboard can't cope, then someone trips the building and you're forced into an emergency upgrade that costs more and gets approved under pressure. Doing it once, properly, with load management is cheaper per outlet than the piecemeal path, and the $125k won't get cheaper if you wait.

Now, the honest counter you should address rather than dismiss, because it'll make your case stronger:

The fairness concern is legitimate. Owners who'll genuinely never use it are subsidising the shared backbone, and for some owners (retirees, fixed incomes) a $2.5-3k lump sum can actually sting even if it's small relative to the asset. Don't wave that away. The answer is partly the value argument (the whole building's resale position improves, which benefits non-EV owners too) and partly structural: you can stage it, or fund the levy over time rather than as one hit.

If any of that co-funding is live, it could cut the per-lot number materially and kill the "prohibitive" argument outright. I'd confirm directly with Sustainability Victoria and Solar Victoria rather than relying on summaries, since these programs open and close in rounds.

In Victoria this needs a 75% special resolution, so the framing matters a lot. **Subject:** Re: 728653T - 40-44 Pakington Street St Kilda - Feasibility study on the installation of EV Chargers

Hi all,

I don't think we should close this out. Doing it now, on the word "prohibitive," is premature and short sighted for the building.

This isn't an "if" question, it's "when." Victoria already mandates EV-ready infrastructure in new builds, adoption keeps climbing, and a building like ours only gets more expensive to fit the longer we leave it. The $125k won't be cheaper in three years, and in the meantime every owner who wants to charge wears the cost on their own.

That's the part "prohibitive" misses. Per owner the backbone is modest. Apportioned by liability it works out to about $22 per entitlement unit, so roughly $1,060 for the smallest lot, around $2,730 for the largest, and most owners between $1,300 and $2,200, as a one-off. Set that against Origin's own figures: installs without the backbone run $10,000+ each, versus $3,000 to $6,000 with it. Declining doesn't save money. It moves a bigger cost onto individual owners later, and it drags on the building's resale and rental appeal as EV-ready becomes what buyers and tenants expect.

The $125k is also only indicative. We haven't asked Origin for the firm quote they offered, and Kimmi's right that we should see what other providers come back with.

So rather than walk away, I'd like us to put a few questions to Origin and to ourselves first:

- Is there a cheaper alternative, from Origin or a competitor?
- Could the resident cost be staged over a few years instead of paid up front?
- Can the OC absorb the backbone over time, or could Origin offer an instalment plan?
- Is a staged rollout viable, part of the capacity now and the rest as we approach it, to spread the cost further?

If the answers still don't stack up, fine, we close it knowing why. But closing it without even asking does every owner a disservice, and it will cost all of us more in the long run.

I'll do the legwork on the quotes and these questions if there's appetite for it.

Thanks,
Nick
